instruction:
State precisely and add a research-grade intuition:

Explain why contacts make robot dynamics hybrid and how this affects control design.
response:
Contact introduces unilateral constraints and discontinuities (impact, stick–slip), yielding hybrid dynamics with mode switches. Controllers must handle constraint forces and mode-dependent models; common approaches include impedance control, MPC with contact constraints, complementarity formulations, and robust controllers that tolerate modeling error.

Example: a 7-DoF arm can reach the same pose with different elbow configurations; constraints choose a feasible posture.

instruction:
Give the statement and one concrete robot example:

Describe Kalman filtering and why linearization is required for the EKF used in robotics.
response:
The Kalman filter provides optimal minimum-variance estimates for linear Gaussian systems through predict and update steps. Robotics models are often nonlinear, so the EKF linearizes the motion/measurement models about the current estimate using Jacobians, approximating the posterior as Gaussian. Consistency depends on good linearization and noise modeling.

Example: a 7-DoF arm can reach the same pose with different elbow configurations; constraints choose a feasible posture.

instruction: Explain sim-to-real gaps in robotic learning and provide mitigation strategies.
response: Sim-to-real gaps arise from unmodeled dynamics, contact/friction variability, sensor noise, and perception differences. Mitigations include domain randomization, system identification, residual learning, conservative policy updates with safety constraints, and online adaptation/monitoring.

instruction: Explain the difference between forward and inverse kinematics, and why inverse kinematics (IK) can be ill-posed.
response: Forward kinematics maps joint variables to an end-effector pose deterministically via the kinematic chain. IK seeks joint variables that realize a desired pose; solutions may be non-unique (redundant robots), nonexistent (unreachable targets), or unstable near singularities. Practical IK adds constraints, damping/regularization, and task hierarchies to make the problem well-posed.

instruction: Define manipulability and explain why near-singular configurations are problematic in robot control.
response: Manipulability characterizes how joint velocities map to end-effector velocities via the Jacobian. Near singularities, the Jacobian loses rank, amplifying velocity/force requirements and making directions of motion poorly controllable. Mitigations include damped least squares, singularity-avoidance terms in planning, and task prioritization.

instruction:
State precisely and add a research-grade intuition:

Define observability in SLAM/estimation and give a robotics example where a state becomes unobservable.
response:
A system is observable if the internal state can be uniquely inferred from inputs and measurements over time. In SLAM, global position and yaw can be unobservable without absolute references; in monocular VIO, metric scale can be ambiguous without sufficient inertial excitation or known-size landmarks. Gauge freedoms are handled by anchoring frames or constraining priors.

What breaks first: EKF consistency degrades with poor noise tuning; smoothing or invariant filtering can improve robustness.

instruction:
Give the statement and one concrete robot example:

Explain the tradeoff between sampling-based planning (RRT*/PRM) and optimization-based planning (TrajOpt/MPC).
response:
Sampling-based planners are probabilistically complete and handle complex constraints but can be slow to produce high-quality smooth trajectories. Optimization-based methods produce smooth trajectories quickly when initialized well but may get stuck in local minima; MPC adds feedback but requires real-time solvability and accurate models.

Example: legged robots switch contact modes; naive linear control can fail without robust impedance or MPC.

instruction: Explain what ROS 2 middleware (DDS) provides and why deterministic behavior is challenging in complex robotic systems.
response: ROS 2 uses DDS for publish/subscribe communication with QoS controls (reliability, durability, deadlines). Determinism is difficult due to OS scheduling jitter, network contention, variable callback execution time, and dynamic memory allocations. Real-time behavior requires RT kernels, bounded allocations, executor tuning, careful QoS, and end-to-end latency measurement.

Define observability in SLAM/estimation and give a robotics example where a state becomes unobservable.
response:
A system is observable if the internal state can be uniquely inferred from inputs and measurements over time. In SLAM, global position and yaw can be unobservable without absolute references; in monocular VIO, metric scale can be ambiguous without sufficient inertial excitation or known-size landmarks. Gauge freedoms are handled by anchoring frames or constraining priors.

Example: legged robots switch contact modes; naive linear control can fail without robust impedance or MPC.

instruction: Describe Kalman filtering and why linearization is required for the EKF used in robotics.
response: The Kalman filter provides optimal minimum-variance estimates for linear Gaussian systems through predict and update steps. Robotics models are often nonlinear, so the EKF linearizes the motion/measurement models about the current estimate using Jacobians, approximating the posterior as Gaussian. Consistency depends on good linearization and noise modeling.

instruction:
State precisely and add a research-grade intuition:

Explain safety in collaborative robotics and list two control-level and two system-level mitigations.
response:
Cobots must limit risk during human interaction. Control-level mitigations: torque/force limits, impedance/admittance control, collision detection using residuals. System-level mitigations: safe-rated monitored stop, speed-and-separation monitoring, certified safety controllers, redundancy, and validated risk assessment processes.

Example: a 7-DoF arm can reach the same pose with different elbow configurations; constraints choose a feasible posture.

instruction: Explain the tradeoff between sampling-based planning (RRT*/PRM) and optimization-based planning (TrajOpt/MPC).
response: Sampling-based planners are probabilistically complete and handle complex constraints but can be slow to produce high-quality smooth trajectories. Optimization-based methods produce smooth trajectories quickly when initialized well but may get stuck in local minima; MPC adds feedback but requires real-time solvability and accurate models.

instruction: Define manipulability and explain why near-singular configurations are problematic in robot control.
response: Manipulability characterizes how joint velocities map to end-effector velocities via the Jacobian. Near singularities, the Jacobian loses rank, amplifying velocity/force requirements and making directions of motion poorly controllable. Mitigations include damped least squares, singularity-avoidance terms in planning, and task prioritization.

instruction: Explain why contacts make robot dynamics hybrid and how this affects control design.
response: Contact introduces unilateral constraints and discontinuities (impact, stick–slip), yielding hybrid dynamics with mode switches. Controllers must handle constraint forces and mode-dependent models; common approaches include impedance control, MPC with contact constraints, complementarity formulations, and robust controllers that tolerate modeling error.

instruction: Compare position control, velocity control, torque control, and impedance control for robot manipulators.
response: Position/velocity control track setpoints via inner loops. Torque control commands joint torques and enables model-based control (e.g., inverse dynamics). Impedance control regulates the relationship between force and motion (stiffness/damping targets) and is essential for contact and interaction; it is often implemented atop torque control.

instruction: Explain what ROS 2 middleware (DDS) provides and why deterministic behavior is challenging in complex robotic systems.
response: ROS 2 uses DDS for publish/subscribe communication with QoS controls (reliability, durability, deadlines). Real-time behavior requires RT kernels, bounded allocations, executor tuning, careful QoS, and end-to-end latency measurement.

instruction: Explain the difference between forward and inverse kinematics, and why inverse kinematics (IK) can be ill-posed.
response: Forward kinematics maps joint variables to an end-effector pose deterministically via the kinematic chain. IK seeks joint variables that realize a desired pose; solutions may be non-unique (redundant robots), nonexistent (unreachable targets), or unstable near singularities. Practical IK adds constraints, damping/regularization, and task hierarchies to make the problem well-posed.

Controllers must handle constraint forces and mode-dependent models; common approaches include impedance control, MPC with contact constraints, complementarity formulations, and robust controllers that tolerate modeling error.

instruction: Describe Kalman filtering and why linearization is required for the EKF used in robotics.
response: The Kalman filter provides optimal minimum-variance estimates for linear Gaussian systems through predict and update steps. Robotics models are often nonlinear, so the EKF linearizes the motion/measurement models about the current estimate using Jacobians, approximating the posterior as Gaussian. Consistency depends on good linearization and noise modeling.

instruction: Define manipulability and explain why near-singular configurations are problematic in robot control.
response: Manipulability characterizes how joint velocities map to end-effector velocities via the Jacobian. Near singularities, the Jacobian loses rank, amplifying velocity/force requirements and making directions of motion poorly controllable. Mitigations include damped least squares, singularity-avoidance terms in planning, and task prioritization.

instruction: Explain the tradeoff between sampling-based planning (RRT*/PRM) and optimization-based planning (TrajOpt/MPC).
response: Sampling-based planners are probabilistically complete and handle complex constraints but can be slow to produce high-quality smooth trajectories. Optimization-based methods produce smooth trajectories quickly when initialized well but may get stuck in local minima; MPC adds feedback but requires real-time solvability and accurate models.

instruction: Explain sim-to-real gaps in robotic learning and provide mitigation strategies.
response: Sim-to-real gaps arise from unmodeled dynamics, contact/friction variability, sensor noise, and perception differences. Mitigations include domain randomization, system identification, residual learning, conservative policy updates with safety constraints, and online adaptation/monitoring.

instruction: Compare position control, velocity control, torque control, and impedance control for robot manipulators.
response: Position/velocity control track setpoints via inner loops. Torque control commands joint torques and enables model-based control (e.g., inverse dynamics). Impedance control regulates the relationship between force and motion (stiffness/damping targets) and is essential for contact and interaction; it is often implemented atop torque control.

instruction:

instruction: Explain the difference between forward and inverse kinematics, and why inverse kinematics (IK) can be ill-posed.

Optimization-based methods produce smooth trajectories quickly when initialized well but may get stuck in local minima; MPC adds feedback but requires real-time solvability and accurate models.

instruction: Define manipulability and explain why near-singular configurations are problematic in robot control.
response: Manipulability characterizes how joint velocities map to end-effector velocities via the Jacobian. Near singularities, the Jacobian loses rank, amplifying velocity/force requirements and making directions of motion poorly controllable. Mitigations include damped least squares, singularity-avoidance terms in planning, and task prioritization.

instruction:
State precisely and add a research-grade intuition:

Define observability in SLAM/estimation and give a robotics example where a state becomes unobservable.
response:
A system is observable if the internal state can be uniquely inferred from inputs and measurements over time. In SLAM, global position and yaw can be unobservable without absolute references; in monocular VIO, metric scale can be ambiguous without sufficient inertial excitation or known-size landmarks. Gauge freedoms are handled by anchoring frames or constraining priors.

Example: legged robots switch contact modes; naive linear control can fail without robust impedance or MPC.

instruction: Explain safety in collaborative robotics and list two control-level and two system-level mitigations.
response: Cobots must limit risk during human interaction. Control-level mitigations: torque/force limits, impedance/admittance control, collision detection using residuals. System-level mitigations: safe-rated monitored stop, speed-and-separation monitoring, certified safety controllers, redundancy, and validated risk assessment processes.

instruction:
State precisely and add a research-grade intuition:

Describe Kalman filtering and why linearization is required for the EKF used in robotics.
response:
The Kalman filter provides optimal minimum-variance estimates for linear Gaussian systems through predict and update steps. Robotics models are often nonlinear, so the EKF linearizes the motion/measurement models about the current estimate using Jacobians, approximating the posterior as Gaussian. Consistency depends on good linearization and noise modeling.

What breaks first: EKF consistency degrades with poor noise tuning; smoothing or invariant filtering can improve robustness.

Explain the limiting assumptions and what breaks first experimentally:

Explain the difference between forward and inverse kinematics, and why inverse kinematics (IK) can be ill-posed.

Explain loop closure in SLAM and why it improves global consistency. Mention one common failure mode.
response: Loop closure detects revisiting a place and adds constraints between current and past poses, converting drift into a global optimization (pose graph). It reduces accumulated error by distributing corrections along the trajectory. Failure mode: perceptual aliasing can cause false loop closures; robust verification and outlier rejection are required.

State the admissibility condition for an A* heuristic and why it implies optimality.
response: A heuristic h is admissible if h(n) never overestimates the true remaining cost: h(n) ≤ h*(n) for all n. Explain point-to-point vs point-to-plane ICP and when point-to-plane converges faster.
